items.say: What's the longest you've ever waited for something?
Maybe it was test results. A phone call. A baby. A job. Or someone to come home. Waiting has a way of stretching time. An hour can feel like a day, and a year can feel like ten.

Today, Christians around the world begin a season that is all about waiting. It's called Advent, from a Latin word that means coming. For the four Sundays before Christmas, we remember how God's people waited, sometimes for centuries, for the Saviour He had promised. And we wait with them, getting our hearts ready to celebrate His birth.

On this first Sunday, many churches light a single candle, the candle of hope. So let's begin there, with one of the most hopeful chapters ever written to people who were tired of waiting. Isaiah chapter 40.
To understand Isaiah 40, it helps to know who it was speaking to.

Earlier chapters of Isaiah warned that Jerusalem would fall. And it did. The city was taken, the temple was destroyed, and many of the people were carried away to Babylon, hundreds of miles from home.

Imagine being one of them. Your home is gone. The place where you worshipped is gone. You're living in a foreign city, among people who don't know your God. One year passes, then ten, then twenty. Children grow up who have never seen Jerusalem.
And a question starts to grow in the quiet. Has God forgotten us?
Isaiah 40 puts that question into words. "Why sayest thou, O Jacob, and speakest, O Israel, My way is hid from the LORD, and my judgment is passed over from my God?"
In plain words: God can't see what I'm going through. He's passed me by.
Maybe you've felt that too.
Now listen to how God begins this chapter. Not with a rebuke. Not with a lecture. With tenderness.
"Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God."
He says it twice, the way a parent says, it's alright, it's alright, to a crying child. And notice the words my people. After everything, after the failure and the exile, they are still His.
Then the chapter turns to a voice, calling out in the wilderness. "The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the LORD, make straight in the desert a highway for our God."

In those days, when a king was coming, workers went ahead to clear the road, to fill in holes and flatten hills so he could travel straight to his people. Isaiah says God Himself is coming, and a road is being made ready for Him.

Centuries later, all four Gospels use these very words to describe John the Baptist, the voice in the wilderness who prepared the way for Jesus. So when we read Isaiah 40 in Advent, we're reading the opening of the Christmas story, written long before Bethlehem.
Next comes one of the most honest passages in the Bible. A voice says, Cry. And the prophet answers, what shall I cry?
"All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field:"
And then: "The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever."

Think about what the exiles had seen. Kingdoms rising and falling. Strong armies, proud cities, famous kings, all fading like grass in the summer heat. Even the things they had loved most had been lost.
But one thing does not fade. The word of God, His promise, stands.

That's the first thing Advent teaches us about waiting. When so much around us changes, hope needs something solid to stand on. Not our feelings, which rise and fall. Not our circumstances, which change week to week. But the promise of a God who keeps His word.
Then Isaiah paints a picture of the God who is coming. First, He is strong. "Behold, the Lord GOD will come with strong hand,"
But the very next image is gentle. "He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and shall gently lead those that are with young."

Strong enough to rule the nations. Gentle enough to carry a lamb. That is the God Advent waits for. And when He came, He came exactly like that: as a baby, laid in a manger, the Good Shepherd who would one day gather the weak and the weary into His arms.
If you're feeling small and tired this season, this picture is for you. He doesn't drive the lambs. He carries them.
And then the chapter reaches its last and most famous verse. Remember the exiles' complaint, that God had passed them by? Here is His answer.
"Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary?"
The God who made the stars doesn't get tired of you.

"Even the youths shall faint and be weary, and the young men shall utterly fall: But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint."

Notice something about that order. Mount up, then run, then walk. You might expect it the other way round, building up to flying. But real life is often like this verse. There are days when hope soars. Days when you can run. And many ordinary days when the most faithful thing you can do is keep walking, and not faint. God promises strength for all three.
So what does it mean to wait upon the Lord?
It doesn't mean sitting still and doing nothing. In the Bible, waiting on God is active. It means looking to Him, trusting Him, staying close to Him while the answer hasn't come yet.

And here's what Isaiah 40 shows us. The strength is not only at the end of the waiting. It's given during it. They that wait shall renew their strength. The waiting room itself becomes the place where God makes us new.
The exiles did go home in the end. But long before they saw Jerusalem again, this promise held them up. And many centuries later, the voice in the wilderness was heard, and the Shepherd came.
As the book of Lamentations puts it: "It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD."
Maybe you're starting Advent this year in your own waiting room. Waiting for healing, for work, for a prodigal to come home, for grief to soften, for a prayer to be answered.

It's important to say gently that hope is not a promise that everything will turn out the way we want, or by Christmas. It's trusting that God has not passed you by, that He sees your way, and that He will give you strength for today's walking.
If your waiting is heavy, please don't carry it alone. Talk to someone you trust, a friend, a pastor, a counselor, or a local helpline. God often sends His comfort through people.
Here's a simple way to begin Advent this week. Each evening, light a candle, or simply sit for a minute in the quiet, and pray one line: Lord, I'm waiting on You. Renew my strength.

And starting on the first of December, we'd love you to wait with us. Every day until Christmas, there'll be a short new prayer here on the channel, one for each day, walking through the promises and the people of the Christmas story. Twenty-four days, twenty-four short stops along the road to Bethlehem.

chapters.title: A prayer for the first week of Advent

items.say: Let's pray.

Everlasting God, Creator of the ends of the earth, You do not faint, and You are never weary of us. Thank You that You did not forget Your people in exile, and that You do not forget us now. As Advent begins, prepare a road in our hearts for You. Where we are tired, renew our strength. Where we feel passed over, remind us that You see our way. Carry the lambs, Lord, and lead us gently. Teach us to wait with hope, and on the ordinary days, help us keep walking and not faint. We wait for You, as Your people did long ago, and we thank You that in Jesus You came. In His name, Amen.
If you're waiting on something this Advent, you can share it in the comments, even in a single word, and we'll pray for you. God bless you, and I'll see you on the road to Christmas.
